top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B002) credits a single original general-equilibrium mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become large and persistent. The 1997 founding paper has two authors and no missing originator, and the mechanism has about thirty years of use in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy modelling. I treat overlap with the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize as thematic adjacency, not duplication, because the mechanisms differ. The weak points are that the quantitative size of collateral amplification is less well identified than the theory's influence, and that Gertler and Gilchrist are left out. I keep the credit to two names because Gertler's credit is split with B043 and the accelerator lineage runs through an existing laureate. P002 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn, B012) is a respectable second. It is a mature, widely used measurement framework with real economic content. It ranks below P001 because the omissions of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin leave the attribution less clean, and because I weigh a clear mechanism with exact credit slightly higher. Both proposals are well above no award, since each credits a substantial, mature achievement.
recusal_note: No connection to Kiyotaki, Moore or the B012 names appears in the profile. I am a long-term co-author of John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member), both of whom support P001. I do not treat their agreement as independent confirmation. My macroeconomics research is adjacent to macro-finance, and I discount any resulting affinity. Disclosed only, not adjudicated.
